stories.headline: Microsoft benchmark finds agents often claim success but leave databases wrong
stories.standfirst: Microsoft's ThinkingBox checks what an AI agent actually changed in a database, not what it said. Across 121,680 trials, the authors say 67% of failures were clean tool calls with wrong values.
body: Microsoft's Copilot Studio team and the data company Toloka published ThinkingBox on 3 October, a benchmark that scores AI agents on the state they leave in a database rather than on their replies. The authors say that across 121,680 trials, 67.24 per cent of failures still called tools cleanly but wrote wrong field values. No outside group has reproduced the numbers.

The write-up, posted on Hugging Face, runs 18 models against 507 business-workflow tasks inside isolated tool sessions. Each task is attempted 20 times, because the authors argue that one success is not reliability. Their stated thesis is that a tool call is not an outcome. Collaborators include researchers at the University of Pittsburgh and Northwestern University.

On a single attempt, Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 leads at 67.16 per cent, the authors report. Moonshot's Kimi-K3 solves 93.89 per cent of tasks at least once but only 13.41 per cent every time. Opus 5.5 and Opus 5 each pass 241 tasks on all 20 tries, the most consistent results in the table.

The authors also price dependability. They say GPT-5.4 has the lowest cost per dependable task at $6.80, while GPT-6 Astra reaches more consistent results, 231 tasks, at $7.45 a task. Roughly four in five failures come from tool handling rather than reasoning, according to the write-up, which suggests the weak point is plumbing, not intelligence.

The framework is MIT-licensed and the benchmark data uses the CDLA-Permissive-2.0 licence. Both are on Hugging Face as microsoft/ThinkingBox-Bench and as an OpenEnv environment under BSD-3-Clause. Because the results come from the benchmark's own authors, and model makers have not commented, the rankings should be read as one team's measurement until others rerun them.

stories.headline: OpenAI's Jalapeño chip has 216 GiB of HBM4 and was tuned by its models
stories.standfirst: OpenAI says its models saved over 13 percent of Jalapeño's die area and lifted one attention kernel from under 1 percent to nearly 90 percent of peak efficiency in 40 hours.
body: OpenAI has put numbers on Jalapeño, the inference chip it designed with Broadcom, in an interview with hardware vice president Richard Ho published on October 4 by the newsletter More Than Moore. The specifications below come from that interview and from OpenAI's account of its HotChips 2026 talk. Nobody outside the company has tested them, and the figures are OpenAI's own.

Each accelerator carries 216 GiB of HBM4 memory at 15.4 terabytes a second, according to the interview. It draws a peak of 700 watts and about 550 watts sustained. Systems group 128 accelerators into one domain and 2,048 into a full system, which OpenAI rates at 27 exaflops of 4-bit compute. Ho described one balanced design for the whole inference job, prefill and decode alike.

OpenAI compared Jalapeño with Nvidia's GB200 and GB300. It claims 1.5 to 1.9 times the performance per watt and 1.7 to 3.6 times lower latency, and up to 104 times better at operating points where it says Nvidia parts struggle. The interview does not say which workloads or models were used, so the comparison cannot be checked from what has been published.

Ho said OpenAI used its own models in the design work, without fine-tuning, and that the internal versions run ahead of public releases. He said they found circuit optimisations worth "over 13% die area". One attention kernel went from "under one percent" of roofline efficiency to nearly 90 percent in 40 hours, he said, a figure the interview does not independently document.

Broadcom handled backend design and IP such as the serial links and chiplets, and Celestica does board and rack integration, per the interview. TSMC supplies the wafers, though no node was disclosed. First silicon arrived in mid-May and a B0 stepping is in qualification. Ho argued for one fungible chip: "if you have a piece of hardware that's more fungible, that seems like a better bet."
An analyst, Jukan, has claimed the chip has yield problems. He cited no source, the claim is unconfirmed, and OpenAI has not commented on it.

stories.headline: Strata repo runs 125B Qwen model on a single gaming GPU
stories.standfirst: Strata, an MIT-licensed runner for Alibaba's 125B Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, has 9,500 GitHub stars after four days. Its author reports 53 to 94 tokens a second on an RTX 5070.
body: Strata, a repository by GitHub user Niko1221, is a runner for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, the 125-billion-parameter open-weight model from Alibaba. By the repository page on Sunday it showed 9,500 stars and 850 forks, and a Hacker News post about it had 76 points and 27 comments. Its first listed release is dated September 30.

The README says the model is split into 24,576 experts, of which roughly ten are used for each token. Strata keeps the most-used experts on the graphics card and leaves the rest in system memory and on the SSD. A smaller draft model proposes tokens that the large one checks in parallel, which the author says speeds decoding by 1.6 to 1.8 times.

The author reports 53 to 94 tokens a second for output on an RTX 5070, and 1,620 to 2,650 tokens a second for reading a prompt, depending on how heavily the model is compressed. The Hacker News title claims 100 tokens a second on an RTX 4090. Those figures are the maker's own, and the paper has not reproduced them.

The requirements are not small. The README asks for 12GB or more of video memory, 32GB of RAM at minimum with 64GB recommended, and about 80GB of free disk. It warns that start-up can freeze a PC for one to three minutes while 35 to 55GB loads into memory. Setup is a one-click script for Windows or Linux, with a browser interface.

The newest release, v0.1.39, dated October 4, adds experimental support for older Nvidia cards, Intel Arc GPUs and CPUs without AVX2. It also adds an OpenAI Responses API endpoint that the release notes say works with Codex CLI, plus parallel conversations. The author says four at once decode 11 percent slower overall.

stories.headline: Seoul orders probe after suspected AI-assisted hacks hit 7 financial firms
stories.standfirst: President Lee Jae-myung ordered a thorough investigation after breaches at four banks and three other lenders, where police found traces of what appears to be an AI penetration-testing tool.
body: South Korean President Lee Jae-myung on Sunday ordered a thorough investigation into data breaches at financial firms. Officials said IP addresses linked to the same attacker turned up at seven of them, according to Digital Today, and investigators believe the attacker used AI tools to automate the intrusions.

Digital Today named Shinhan Bank, KB Kookmin Bank, Hana Bank, BNK Busan Bank, Hyundai Capital, Yegaram Savings Bank and Welcome Savings Bank. The Korea Times put Shinhan's exposure at about 25,000 customers and Yegaram's at about 40,000. Leaked fields included names, phone numbers, annual income and loan limits, and in some cases resident registration numbers.

The AI link is the contested part. The Korea Times reported that police found traces of a Chinese-language AI penetration-testing tool on a server, with a page title that translates as an AI autonomous penetration testing console. It tied the tool tentatively to an open-source system called ARTEX AI. No other outlet reviewed by this paper names the tool.

Cybersecurity News noted that investigators have not publicly established that one group carried out every breach, or that AI independently completed each attack. It said the intrusions came through loan-agent websites and employee support systems, not customer-facing banking apps, and that no customer transaction information leaked in those incidents.

Financial Services Commission chairman Lee Eog-weon told the industry to stay on the highest alert, the Korea Times reported, and Digital Today quoted him calling for defences in which AI is used against AI attacks. Authorities warned that the exposed data could be used for voice phishing and text-message scams.

stories.headline: Coding-agent add-ons ponytail and caveman pass 100,000 GitHub stars
stories.standfirst: Ponytail claims 54 percent fewer lines of code and caveman claims 33 percent fewer input tokens. Both are free add-ons for coding agents, at 154,000 and 110,000 stars.
body: Two open-source add-ons for AI coding agents sit among the most-starred and fastest-growing repositories on GitHub, according to an October 4 trend report and the repositories' own pages. Ponytail, by DietrichGebert, showed 154,200 stars and 8,300 forks, and gained 1,281 stars in a day. Caveman, by JuliusBrussee, showed 109,700 stars.

Ponytail's README says it makes agents write minimal code, running a checklist before generating anything: does the code need to exist, is it already in the codebase, does the standard library cover it. The README says benchmarks on real Claude Code sessions showed 54 percent fewer lines on average, a 20 percent cost cut and 27 percent faster runs. Those figures are the project's own.

Caveman, created in April, takes a different route. Its README says a skill rewrites agent replies in terse, answer-first sentences, and a local proxy compresses what agents read, such as logs and CSV files, by about 98.5 to 99.1 percent. The README claims 33.2 percent fewer input tokens across full sessions, with all 18 answers still correct. This paper has not tested either claim.

A third project, Agent-Reach by Panniantong, was the day's biggest gainer in the trend report, adding 1,696 stars. Its README says it gives agents one command-line tool to read Twitter, Reddit, YouTube and other sites with no API fees, switching to a backup route when one fails. The page showed 90,300 stars and an MIT licence.

Ponytail and caveman say they work with Claude Code and Codex, among others, with ponytail listing more than 20 agents and caveman more than 30. The star counts are public, but stars measure interest and not use, and the efficiency numbers come from the authors' own runs.

stories.headline: Open-source kit lets Claude Code mod single-player PC games
stories.standfirst: The universal-modder repo has 2,800 stars and 244 forks four days after launch. Its author says an agent can use it to reverse-engineer a game and add art, 3D models and audio.
body: A GitHub project called universal-modder, published on 30 September by developer rehan-remade, had 2,810 stars and 244 forks when this paper checked on Sunday. The repository describes itself as skills and tools that let Claude Code mod almost any PC game the user owns.

According to the README, the workflow runs from reconnaissance and reverse engineering to generating art, 3D models and audio through the fal MCP server, then in-game testing and recording showcase videos. A command-line tool called um has more than 40 commands for scanning games, generating assets and recording gameplay. The project is MIT licensed.

The README lists three example mods. A Terraria add-on has a tactical nuke, a chain-lightning rifle and a two-phase Drone Mothership boss. An Age of Empires II civilisation, San Franciscans, gets a Robotaxi unit and a Transamerica Pyramid wonder. A third puts Minecraft inside GTA V story mode. This paper has not run any of them.

The README says the kit also works with Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI and GitHub Copilot. It sets limits: the project says it refuses to inject into online games with anti-cheat, write cheats against other players or bypass DRM and ownership checks, and it needs single-player games or self-hosted servers. How well it works beyond the author's own examples has not been independently reported.

stories.headline: Perplexity says its decision API cleared Pokémon FireRed's Elite Four
stories.standfirst: Chief executive Aravind Srinivas posted a video of the run, saying the API answered in a median 592 milliseconds and the whole run cost an estimated $0.028.
body: Perplexity chief executive Aravind Srinivas posted a video on Sunday of Pokémon FireRed's Elite Four and Champion cleared "in one shot", with decisions made by Perplexity's Decisions API. The clip and the figures come from his post, and nobody outside the company has verified the run.

Srinivas listed the run's stats: a median API response of 592 milliseconds, a 95th-percentile response of 987 milliseconds, 96.4 percent of responses under one second, and 137 live API calls. He put the estimated inference cost of the whole run at $0.028.

Perplexity's documentation describes the Decisions API as returning probabilities instead of text: yes-or-no answers, a pick from a list of options, or a score on a rubric. It runs on a single model, pplx-decider-v1-27b, priced at $0.04 per million input tokens with free output. The docs do not mention Pokémon.

The post does not say how the game state reached the API, how long the run took in real time, or whether the Elite Four were fought with a team prepared in advance. The documentation says requests of a few hundred input tokens answer in under two seconds, which fits the order of magnitude Srinivas reports.

stories.headline: Aleph Alpha says Chinese models give balanced answers 17 to 41 percent
stories.standfirst: Aleph Alpha says Qwen, DeepSeek and Kimi answered 967 taboo-topic questions in a balanced way only 17 to 41 percent of the time, against 70 to 92 percent for Western models. The Decoder reported it.
body: Chinese AI models often follow the party line on politically sensitive questions, according to a study by the German company Aleph Alpha, which The Decoder reported on Saturday. Aleph Alpha built a benchmark of 967 hand-picked taboo topics, such as Tiananmen and Taiwan, and scored each answer as balanced or not.

The company says models from Alibaba (Qwen), DeepSeek and Moonshot AI (Kimi) produced balanced answers in only 17 to 41 percent of cases. Western models in the comparison, Claude Sonnet 5 and Mistral Small, reached 70 to 92 percent, The Decoder said. It adds that DeepSeek V4 Pro refused about two-thirds of the sensitive questions.

The bias also leaks into topics beyond China, the report says. When asked about censorship in the United States, Qwen 3.6 answered that "many countries, including China, also manage information to ensure social stability and national security," according to the quoted example. The Decoder also says a separate study by the Central European Institute of Asian Studies reached similar findings.

Aleph Alpha sells "sovereign AI" to governments, so it has a commercial interest in separating its models from Chinese rivals, as The Decoder notes. The benchmark's questions and scoring method were not independently checked, and we have not seen the full study. The Chinese labs named had not commented in the report. The Decoder is the only outlet we found with the account so far.

stories.headline: Google to cut free Gemini users to Flash-Lite and give AI Pro Deep Think
stories.standfirst: Google is restricting which Gemini models free and $4.99 AI Plus users can open, leaving free accounts with only Flash-Lite. The $19.99 AI Pro tier gains Deep Think, according to 9to5Google.
body: Google is about to limit which Gemini models people can use by plan, 9to5Google reported on 3 October, citing a Google support document. Free users would keep only Flash-Lite and lose Flash and Pro. The Decoder, which reported the same change, says it starts in October. Neither outlet gives Google's own announcement, and the paper has not seen one.

AI Plus, the $4.99 monthly plan, would get Flash-Lite and Flash but no Pro, according to both outlets. AI Pro at $19.99 and the AI Ultra plans at $99.99 and $199.99 would keep all three models. The Decoder frames the move as a step toward the freemium split OpenAI uses in ChatGPT, where the strongest models sit behind payment.

The one gain is for AI Pro subscribers, who 9to5Google says will get Deep Think, the slow reasoning mode until now reserved for the Ultra plans. The report adds that the Gemini app will also add effort settings from low to high, as Google AI Studio has. The support document says higher effort improves answers but uses more of a user's limit.

The Decoder suggests the tiering could set the stage for Gemini 4 Argon, the model Google announced on 30 September and has so far offered only to a program for trusted cyber defenders. 9to5Google notes that Google has not said whether Argon would count as a Pro model or sit above Pro. That is the open question for subscribers.

The Decoder also argues that most casual users do not know which Gemini model they are running, so the practical effect may be small for them. Power users who rely on Flash or Pro for free would have to pay. Google has not commented in either report, and the exact start date was not confirmed by both outlets.

stories.headline: Meta opens Muse Gadgets, a DIY kit for building AI hardware
stories.standfirst: Meta says its Apache 2.0 kit pairs ESP32 firmware and a Linux SDK with its Muse agent, and 5,000 USB-C Home Link devices are due within weeks.
body: Meta has announced Muse Gadgets, an open-source project that lets hobbyists build their own AI hardware, The Decoder reported on 3 October. It includes firmware for ESP32 boards and a Linux SDK for connecting homemade devices to Muse, Meta's AI agent. The code is Apache 2.0 licensed, and the project has a Discord community.

Meta also built a device of its own. The Muse Home Link is a small USB-C gadget that connects Muse to a home network, letting it control any device with an HTTPS interface, such as a TV or speaker, according to Meta. The company says 5,000 units have been produced and should ship within weeks, free for Muse subscribers while supplies last.

The project is also listed on Product Hunt, which describes it as Meta's open-source kit for building your own AI gadgets. We found no independent builds or tests of the firmware or the SDK, so what they can do rests on Meta's description. The Decoder suggests Meta may use the project to learn which form factors people actually want, a reading the company has not stated.

Muse itself has become a hit with consumers, Wired reported on 3 October, with millions downloading the assistant and connecting it to bank accounts, messages or health data. Researchers have since extracted its internal instructions, which Meta told Wired it meant to make accessible in the interest of transparency. The Gadgets kit would extend that agent from the phone into the home.

stories.headline: White House names Clayton to lead AI 'Super Intelligence Force'
stories.standfirst: Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton will lead a White House task force with 120 days to report on AI's risks and opportunities, the Wall Street Journal reported.
body: The White House has created a task force to examine AI's risks and opportunities, the Wall Street Journal reported on Saturday. It is to recommend what role the federal government should play in overseeing the technology, with a report due within 120 days. Reuters relayed the account, which cites the task force's head, Jay Clayton.

The group is known as the "Super Intelligence Force", and Clayton, who heads the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, told the Journal he would lead it. He would effectively serve as President Donald Trump's AI czar, according to Reuters. The report also cites a senior White House official. Bloomberg carried the story the same day, attributing it to the Journal.

The appointment follows earlier reporting. CBS News said on Thursday, citing sources, that Clayton was likely to be Trump's pick for AI czar while staying director of national intelligence. The commentator Andrew Curran wrote on X late Saturday that the task force had been renamed the SI Force, citing the Journal.

The Reuters account does not say who else sits on the task force, what budget or legal authority it has, or whether its report would bind agencies. We opened Reuters' version, not the Journal's paywalled article, and found no White House statement confirming the name. The 120-day clock would run into early next year if it started now.

stories.headline: Willison says coding agents mean pay-per-use services need hard spending caps
stories.standfirst: Simon Willison argues cloud services should cut off at a set bill by default, since agents make surprise bills of thousands of dollars easier. AWS and Google Cloud only just added caps.
body: Developer Simon Willison argued on 3 October that pay-by-usage services and APIs should ship with default hard budget caps, a setting that stops service and returns errors once a monthly limit is reached. His post says soft caps that only send warning emails fail, because people sleep through them while bills grow.

Willison ties the proposal to coding agents. In his telling, they make it easier to deploy applications that can generate large, unexpected charges. He puts the typical damage at several hundred or several thousand dollars, with surprise bills above $10,000 the point where it becomes serious, and says some developers avoid AWS for personal projects out of fear of exactly that.

He credits two providers with moving. AWS launched spending limits on 16 September, he writes: when usage reaches the cap, the project pauses for the month, though he says the feature is limited to select customers. Google Cloud added Spend Caps in July, letting users cap spending on specific services inside a project.

Willison proposes that turning a cap off should need explicit wording: "Remove the budget cap. My application will not be shut down if I exceed the configured budget limit, and I will be responsible for subsequent charges." The post is opinion, not a vendor announcement. Neither AWS nor Google has commented, as far as the sources show.

The argument may matter most to people running agents unattended. A hard cap could turn a runaway loop into an error message instead of an invoice, but it also takes the service down, which is why Willison says it should be the default. He does not say which other providers lack such limits.
